title: Conditional sentence for police officer convicted in woman's custody death
subtitle: A London police officer convicted of failing to provide the necessaries of life in the 2016 custody death of an Indigenous woman has avoided jail time.
article: A London police officer convicted of failing to provide the necessaries of life in the 2016 custody death of an Indigenous woman has avoided jail time.

Const. Nicholas Doering on Friday was given an 18-month conditional sentence - half of it spent on house arrest - for his role in the Sept. 6, 2016, death of Debra Chrisjohn, a mother of 11 who died in police custody.
Chrisjohn's sister Cindy said she was disappointed by the conditional sentence.

"I feel like this sentence does not affect Doering in any type of way. It really does not send any type of deterrence as the judge mentioned. I felt like she was saying the right things about the distrust with the police, and how Indigenous lives matter. Having stated all of that, the sentence is not acceptable," Cindy Chrisjohn wrote in a statement.
"Seven years of being stuck in the justice system . . . to receive no justice, no change, no accountability. This to me is just a continuance to show there is no justice for Indigenous peoples."

Doering originally was sentenced to 12 months in jail in 2020 after he was found guilty of criminal negligence causing death and failing to provide the necessaries of life, but the Ontario Court of Appeal overturned the criminal negligence causing death conviction last year and ordered Superior Court Justice Renee Pomerance to resentence Doering.
The Crown asked for a jail sentence of six to nine months, while the defence wanted a conditional sentence of six to 12 months.

"I did not believe that anything less than real jail would suffice for the offences including criminal negligence. The case in now materially different and I believe that a conditional sentence can achieve the relevant objectives of sentencing in the current context. These include not only deterrence and denunciation but also rehabilitation and consideration of Mr. Doering's fragile state of health," Pomerance said.

"This decision should not be seen as devaluing Ms. Chrisjohn's life. To the contrary, the events in question were tragic and resulted in the death of a woman who was loved by many and who deserved to be treated with more dignity than was offered to her. However, the purpose of a sentence is not to quantify loss of life. No sentence could realistically bear that burden."

Doering had arrested Chrisjohn, 39, in east London after she was found walking into traffic while high on crystal methamphetamine. He transferred her to Elgin OPP custody on an outstanding arrest warrant, falsely telling OPP officers Chrisjohn had been medically assessed by paramedics, court heard.

Shortly after the OPP took Chrisjohn into custody, paramedics were called to the Elgin OPP detachment, where they found her motionless on her cell floor. Chrisjohn died later in hospital. A post-mortem determined she died from cardiac arrest linked to crystal meth use, court heard.
Pomerance said the case represents a breach of public trust imposed on police officers to protect all members of the community and reflects a disregard for the welfare of a vulnerable woman.
"The victim was viewed as more of a nuisance than a human being who required medical assistance," she said.

Pomerance highlighted the toll the legal proceeding has taken on Doering, who has been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder, and how a jail sentence would have a harsher impact on a police officer.

"He has experienced significant collateral consequences as the result of these proceedings. He has lost his career," she said of Doering. "The case has attracted a considerable attention in the media, including social media. There has been public shaming of the accused."

Doering initially was placed on administrative duties in July 2017 after Ontario's police watchdog, the Special Investigations Unit, charged him and OPP Const. Mark McKillop in Chrisjohn's death. The charges against McKillop, who testified at Doering's trial, later were withdrawn.
Doering has been suspended with pay since he was sentenced on Sept. 21, 2020, and briefly taken into custody before being granted bail after his appeal was filed.

A weapons ban initially was included in Doering's sentence, but defence lawyer Alan Gold argued against it, noting the order was stayed by the appeal court and weapons had nothing to do with the crime.
"My client's possession of firearms is very significant and personal and related to his life," Gold said. "He has hunting firearms, as does his family."
Pomerance agreed to withdrawn the weapons ban after the Crown conceded the prohibition shouldn't apply to the case.

Doering was supposed to be sentenced in July , but the hearing was adjourned after Gold asked Pomerance to overturn Doering's conviction on failing to provide the necessaries of life, a decision she said she wasn't authorized to make.

"We obviously welcome the elimination of a sentence of actual imprisonment but we are considering our other options as there may be a serious question regarding (Pomerance's) conclusion that she lacks jurisdiction to consider our arguments," Gold said in a statement after the sentencing hearing.
